EFTA comprises Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, which are not EU members. The agreement was signed in Hanoi by senior representatives of the four EFTA states, including Swiss President Guy Parmelin, and by Vietnam's Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung, according to an EFTA document. Its entry into force is pending, the document said.
Also read: Vietnam's export boom offers India six lessons for growth
Bilateral trade between EFTA and Vietnam was EUR 4.8 billion in 2025, with a surplus of EUR 2.5 billion in Vietnam's favour, up from EUR 0.5 billion a decade earlier, according to EFTA. Electrical machinery, footwear and apparel, and mechanical machinery were the top imports from Vietnam.
India's Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA) with EFTA was signed on March 10, 2024, and came into force on October 1, 2025. EFTA offered market access on 92.2% of its tariff lines, covering 99.6% of India's exports. India opened 82.7% of its tariff lines, covering 95.3% of EFTA's exports, according to the Press Information Bureau (PIB).
Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), said the deal will not affect India's exports. "EFTA countries levy zero tariffs on industrial products, so deal with Vietnam or any other country including India offers no additional tariff advantage in these markets," he said. Competition will depend on product quality, price and delivery reliability, he said.
Normal route or FTA route
EFTA's free trade dashboard says Iceland and Norway abolished tariffs on most industrial imports on their own, and Switzerland and Liechtenstein did so from January 1, 2024.
Preferences under an FTA are not automatic, the dashboard says. Importers must claim them, and goods must meet the agreement's rules of origin. It calculates preference utilisation only on the subset of trade where a preferential margin exists. Its data covers 2018 to 2024, before India's pact took effect.
India's exports to EFTA
Dhar said Vietnam's duty-free access to EFTA countries poses a significant challenge to India's ambition of increasing its presence there. He said Indian exporters have struggled to use the market access opportunities since the agreement was signed. Exports fell nearly 11% in 2025-26 and by over 9% in January to July 2026 over 2025, he said.
The Commerce Ministry said in May that India's exports to Switzerland, its largest EFTA partner, crossed $1.2 billion in 2025-26.
Products that overlap
India's exports to EFTA in 2024-25 included engineering goods worth $315 million, up 18% from the year before, according to the PIB. Dhar said telephones and electronics products, and textiles and clothing, have been among Vietnam's major exports to EFTA in recent years, and that India has considerable competitive strengths in these industries.
The European Union angle
EU-Vietnam goods trade was EUR 76 billion in 2025, and the EU's deficit was EUR 51.7 billion, according to the Commission. Machinery and appliances made up more than half of EU imports from Vietnam, followed by footwear and textiles.
On September 11, the Commission sent proposals to the EU Council seeking authorisation to sign and conclude the India deal.
India's Commerce Ministry put India's goods exports to the EU at $75.85 billion in 2024-25. It said $33 billion of India's labour-intensive exports, including textiles and leather and footwear, face EU duties of 4% to 26% and will move to zero at entry into force. It valued India's textile and apparel exports to the EU at $7.2 billion.
The $100 billion investment goal
Under Article 7.1(3) of TEPA, the EFTA states "shall aim to increase" foreign direct investment into India by $50 billion within 10 years of the agreement taking effect, and by another $50 billion in the following five years, according to the agreement text.
Also read: Vietnam's export triumph: How a small nation beat China and India to become America's top trade partner
The PIB describes the commitments as binding. Under Article 7.7, a sub-committee will review progress at five, 10 and 15 years. If the objectives are not met by the final review, India can seek consultations and, if they fail, take temporary measures to rebalance its tariff concessions, the text says.
Srivastava described the commitment as "just an aspirational target tied to India's high GDP growth and high returns to EFTA companies in India." Dhar said: "These are still early days to assess whether there has been any forward movement on this promise."
Data from the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) show cumulative FDI equity inflow from Switzerland, the largest EFTA source of investment in India, at $11.32 billion from April 2000 to March 2026. It was $10.88 billion up to June 2025, a rise of about $440 million.

With a gross domestic product (GDP) of US$19.4 trillion, the EU is currently the world's third largest economy and accounts for approximately 14% of total global trade.
Since the official establishment of diplomatic relations on November 28, 1990, Vietnam-EU relations have developed increasingly positively. Therefore, the upgrading of relations to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership during the visit of European Council President António Costa to Vietnam in January 2026 is a historic milestone, making Vietnam the first ASEAN country to have the highest level of relationship with the EU, demonstrating a high level of political trust and shared strategic vision in this stage of development.
According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade, after six years of implementation, the EVFTA agreement has proven highly effective, making Vietnam the EU's largest trading partner in ASEAN. Vietnam's main export partners within the EU bloc are concentrated in the Netherlands , Germany, France, Italy, Belgium, and Spain, accounting for over 70% of total export turnover to the EU. Of this, exports to the EU will average US$47.71 billion per year, with an average growth rate of approximately 10.2% per year; imports from the EU will average US$16.32 billion per year, with an average growth rate of approximately 4.2% per year.

Notably, among European businesses involved in bilateral trade, half reported directly benefiting from the EVFTA tariff preferences; two-thirds of this group recorded measurable financial savings.
August 1st, 2026 marked the 6th anniversary of the official entry into force of the EVFTA Agreement. Although a brief chapter in the 36-year journey of establishing formal diplomatic relations between the EU and Vietnam, this agreement has had a significant impact on the bilateral economic corridor. Specifically, the agreement has reshaped trade flows, fostered business confidence, and positioned Vietnam as one of Europe's leading economic anchors in Asia.

articles.full_text:
Strategic HR
Not every layoff is about AI: 5 forces driving Singapore’s workforce cuts despite employment growth
Although technology can change the nature of work, AI should not automatically be treated as the primary explanation for every round of job cuts.
As companies announce job cuts, artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being blamed for the changing employment scenarios. But is technology the primary reason behind workforce reductions?
Singapore’s recent cases suggest the picture is more complicated, with production requirements, cost pressures, ownership changes and financial distress also influencing decisions.
Ubisoft plans to cut 70 positions at its Singapore studio as it aligns production capacity with upcoming projects.
Restaurant group Crystal Jade has issued termination notices to around 120 workers as part of a restructuring ahead of a proposed sale.
Meanwhile, True Fitness and True Yoga have ceased operations in Singapore, and advertising technology company The Trade Desk has reduced its global workforce, including employees in Singapore.
Another case, Bakery chain Twelve Cupcakes ceased operations in October 2025, leaving 80 employees unpaid. MOM issued a warning on 1 April 2026, finding that the closure stemmed from severe financial distress rather than deliberate salary non-payment.
These cases point to different business circumstances. While some companies may be aligning their workforce with production requirements, others are reviewing expenditure, preparing for ownership changes or dealing with financial difficulties.
Singapore’s wider employment figures offer a contrasting picture. Total employment grew by 57,300 in 2025, while the employment rate among residents aged 15 and above reached 65.7%. In the second quarter of 2026, employment increased by a further 11,400, marking the 19th consecutive quarter of growth. The overall unemployment rate stood at 1.9%.
The figures highlight an important distinction: employment growth across the economy does not prevent individual businesses from reducing headcount or discontinuing operations. Workforce decisions are often driven by company-specific requirements rather than a single economy-wide trend.
1. Matching headcount to production requirements
Workforce requirements are closely linked to the volume and nature of work a company expects to undertake. When production plans change, organisations may need to reassess staffing levels and the capabilities required to deliver future projects.
Ubisoft’s decision to align production capacity with upcoming projects highlights how staffing needs can change as project portfolios and business priorities are reviewed.
For companies operating across multiple markets or product lines, workforce requirements may vary according to project timelines, demand forecasts and investment decisions. A team built around previous production needs may no longer reflect the resources required for future work.
The priority is to connect workforce planning with operational forecasts. This involves assessing upcoming projects, identifying critical capabilities and determining whether existing teams are aligned with anticipated workloads.
The challenge is to ensure that workforce decisions reflect actual business requirements, while considering the implications for productivity, continuity and future growth.
2. Reviewing operating costs to protect margins
Rising operating expenses and pressure on profitability can prompt companies to review how resources are allocated across their businesses.
Workforce expenditure is one component of this assessment. Depending on the company's circumstances, management may review team structures, staffing requirements, operating processes and spending across functions to determine where costs can be controlled without undermining essential operations.
Singapore employers are also facing pressure from rising manpower costs. The Singapore National Employers Federation’s Wage and Employment Outlook Survey 2026/2027 found that 83% of surveyed employers identified rising manpower costs as a challenge, compared with 79% in 2025.
However, this finding reflects a broader employer concern and does not establish that rising manpower costs caused the job cuts at any of the companies mentioned above.
The objective is to understand how workforce expenditure relates to business output and financial performance.
This requires evaluating whether current staffing arrangements support operational requirements and whether alternative processes or resource allocations could improve efficiency.
Cost reduction alone should not determine the outcome. Decisions also need to account for their potential effects on service quality, institutional knowledge, delivery capacity and the organisation’s ability to pursue future opportunities.
3. Preparing for a change in business ownership
When ownership changes are being considered, management may assess how the business should operate under a future ownership structure. This can involve reviewing existing functions, identifying overlapping responsibilities and determining which activities are essential to the business.
Restaurant group Crystal Jade has issued termination notices as part of a restructuring ahead of a proposed sale. The development illustrates how workforce decisions can occur alongside changes in ownership plans.
However, the precise rationale for the company's workforce decisions should not be assumed without further confirmation. A proposed sale does not, by itself, establish why particular roles are affected.
These situations require careful coordination between financial planning, operational management and workforce decisions.
Management needs to understand the implications of proposed changes for business continuity, staffing requirements and the organisation’s future operating model.
Clear communication and appropriate planning are also important when decisions affect employees, customers, suppliers and other stakeholders.
4. Addressing financial distress and the risk of business closure
Not every company reducing its workforce is preparing for its “next phase of growth”. In some cases, financial distress can leave businesses unable to sustain operations.
The closure of Twelve Cupcakes illustrates the distinction between a planned workforce restructuring and a business that can no longer continue operating.
The bakery chain ceased operations leaving 80 employees unpaid. Following an investigation, MOM determined that the closure resulted from severe financial distress rather than a deliberate attempt to avoid salary payments.
This case highlights how financial difficulties can extend beyond workforce planning to the company's ability to meet its employment obligations.
Monitoring financial health is therefore essential. Cash flow, outstanding liabilities, operating expenditure and revenue performance can provide important indicators of whether a business can sustain its current operations.
When financial distress becomes serious, management must work with relevant legal and insolvency professionals to understand its obligations and manage the closure process appropriately.
Salary payments and other employment matters must be handled in accordance with applicable requirements.
The case also demonstrates why workforce reductions should not automatically be attributed to AI or technological change. A company may cease operations because of financial circumstances that are unrelated to automation.
5. Reassessing business priorities and resource allocation
Workforce restructuring can also reflect a broader reassessment of where a company intends to invest and how it plans to allocate resources.
The Trade Desk, reduced its global workforce, including employees in Singapore. True Fitness and True Yoga, meanwhile, have ceased operations in Singapore. These developments represent different business circumstances and should not be treated as evidence of a common underlying cause.
For companies continuing to operate, changes in business priorities may prompt management to review which markets, products or functions require investment. Organisations may redirect resources towards selected activities while reducing spending elsewhere.
In other cases, a business may no longer be able to sustain its operations, making closure rather than restructuring the relevant outcome.
The task is to connect workforce decisions with a clear assessment of business priorities. This includes determining which activities are essential, where resources can deliver the greatest value and whether the organisation has the financial and operational capacity to support its plans.
Such assessments need to distinguish between decisions intended to improve an ongoing business and situations in which the business itself is no longer viable.
The two require different approaches to financial planning, workforce management and stakeholder communication.
Takeaway
Singapore’s employment growth and company-level job cuts are not contradictory. National employment figures reflect the combined performance of businesses across industries, while individual companies make workforce decisions according to their own operating requirements and financial circumstances.
They also show why AI should not automatically be treated as the primary explanation for every round of job cuts. Although technology can change the nature of work and influence staffing decisions, the reasons behind each case need to be assessed using company-specific evidence.
For business leaders, the priority is to make workforce planning part of wider business strategy.

articles.title: To achieve rapid growth, we must unlock resources for production. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: To achieve rapid growth, we must unlock resources for production.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
(Newspaper and Public Opinion Newspaper) To promote economic growth, the issue is not only about mobilizing more resources but also about improving the efficiency of public investment, removing barriers to accessing capital for businesses, and maximizing the effectiveness of private investment resources. How can capital flows truly be transformed into productive capacity, creating more value for the economy and promoting rapid and sustainable growth? A reporter from the Newspaper and Public Opinion Newspaper interviewed National Assembly representative, Associate Professor Dr. Nguyen Ngoc Son (Hai Phong City delegation) on this topic.
+ Distinguished delegates, to achieve high growth targets, besides mobilizing resources, the crucial issue is the efficient use of capital. In your opinion, how should we innovate the way we allocate and evaluate the effectiveness of public investment to not only accelerate disbursement but also create new production capacity and a ripple effect for the economy ?
- I believe it's time to change the question posed regarding public investment: it's not just about "how much has been disbursed" but "what has that capital generated?". In the first nine months of 2026, GDP grew by 9.01%, with the third quarter reaching 9.95%, the highest in many years, and public investment made a very important contribution. However, by the beginning of October, nationwide disbursement had only reached about 63.8% of the plan, and the main reason remains that many projects lack the necessary investment procedures. This means the bottleneck lies in the preparation phase, not just the implementation phase.
Therefore, in my opinion, innovation is needed in three areas. Firstly, in the allocation stage, we must shift completely from a "even distribution" mindset to a "selective selection" mindset. Capital must be concentrated on projects that create new production capacity and attract other investments: inter-regional transport infrastructure, seaports, logistics, energy, digital infrastructure, data centers, and shared laboratories serving science , technology, and innovation, in line with Resolution 57-NQ/TW. Projects that are not well-prepared should not be allocated capital, avoiding the situation where allocated funds are left waiting for procedures to be completed.
Secondly, in the evaluation phase, a set of indicators measuring output and impact is needed, not just progress. A completed road project should be evaluated based on the reduction in transportation costs, the volume of goods transported, the number of businesses, and the amount of private capital attracted to the surrounding area. The government has set forth a policy of accounting for socio-economic efficiency before, during, and after investment; the important thing is to quantify and publicly disclose these results on a digital data platform, so that the National Assembly, People's Councils, and the people can jointly monitor them.
Thirdly, there's the issue of accountability and motivation. Disbursement results and project effectiveness must be linked to the responsibility of the project leader, and funds should be promptly reallocated from slow-performing areas to those that are performing well. At the same time, we need to protect officials who dare to think and act for the common good. I want to emphasize: leaving funds idle in accounts is also a waste and cannot be considered "safe." Inaction should also be considered a shortcoming.
+ In reality, many businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), still find it difficult to access capital, while bank financing is still available. So, what bottlenecks need to be addressed in the credit assessment mechanism, collateral requirements, and capital absorption capacity to enable businesses to expand production and operations, sir?
- This is a paradox that needs to be faced directly. By the end of September 2026, total credit outstanding in the system will reach approximately 20.75 million billion VND, an increase of 11.59% compared to the end of 2025; the State Bank of Vietnam has also implemented a credit program for growth drivers and small and medium-sized enterprises with interest rates lower than the general average. That is, capital is available, policies are in place, but the flow of capital is still not evenly distributed to the small business sector. In my opinion, there are three main bottlenecks.
You may also like
The first bottleneck is that credit assessment still heavily relies on collateral, especially real estate. Small businesses and innovative startups often don't own much land or factory space, but they do have orders, cash flow, and technology. There needs to be a strong shift towards lending based on cash flow and data: electronic invoices, tax data, payment history, and transactions on digital platforms. To achieve this, data must be connected and shared between tax authorities, social insurance agencies, credit information systems, and banks, while ensuring the protection of personal data.
The second bottleneck is the legal framework for new types of collateral. Intellectual property rights, research results, accounts receivable, inventory, machinery, equipment, etc., all have value but are difficult to accept due to the lack of a convenient mechanism for valuation, registration, and handling of these assets. This is an area that the National Assembly and the Government need to continue to improve, while also enhancing the capacity of credit guarantee funds for small and medium-sized enterprises, which are still operating rather sluggishly in many localities.
The third bottleneck lies on both sides. On the bank side, credit officers still have a fear of responsibility when lending without collateral; it is necessary to clearly distinguish: adhering to the correct procedures and conducting honest assessments will prevent objective business risks from being attributed to individuals, and certainly not criminalized. On the business side, the ability to absorb capital is limited due to opaque accounting records and unconvincing business plans. Therefore, along with credit, businesses need support in management, accounting, digital transformation , and opening up additional capital channels such as venture capital funds and capital markets, so that businesses do not rely solely on banks.
+ Public investment can create infrastructure and pave the way for private investment, while businesses are the direct force creating products, jobs, and added value for the economy. According to you, what breakthrough solutions are needed to connect these two resources, unlock capital flows into production and business, and create momentum for rapid and sustainable growth?
- I envision public investment as "seed capital," while private investment is the "mainstream flow." Seed capital is only meaningful when it attracts the mainstream flow. To connect these two resources, I believe several groundbreaking solutions are needed.
Firstly, planning and information must come first. The list of public investment projects, infrastructure plans, and surrounding land funds must be publicly available, transparent, and stable, so that businesses can proactively plan investments in factories, warehouses, and related services. At the same time, the Transport-Oriented Development (TOD) model should be strongly applied, exploiting the added value of land around infrastructure projects for reinvestment, instead of allowing that value to fall into the hands of speculators.
Secondly, we need to promote substantive public-private partnerships, with clear risk-sharing mechanisms, respected contracts, and prompt dispute resolution. Investors will only invest long-term capital when they believe that the State's commitments will be fulfilled.
You may also like
Thirdly, use public investment and public procurement to create a market for domestic businesses, especially technology companies. When the State orders scientific and technological products, prioritizing materials, equipment, and digital solutions produced by Vietnamese businesses in infrastructure projects, public capital not only builds the projects but also nurtures production capacity. This is also the spirit set forth in Resolution 57-NQ/TW and Resolution 68-NQ/TW on the development of the private economy.
Fourth, and this is a fundamental condition, institutional reforms must continue: substantially reducing administrative procedures and business conditions, shifting strongly from pre-approval to post-approval, and ensuring a stable and predictable legal environment. Reduced compliance costs and legal risks represent a huge intangible asset freed up for businesses.
In Hai Phong , we clearly see this: the development of port infrastructure, highways, and industrial zones has led to a strong wave of investment in manufacturing and logistics. This experience shows that when the State plays a proactive and pioneering role, maintaining transparent and stable rules of the game, businesses will be the force that transforms capital into products, jobs, and sustainable growth.
